hero.label: IDENTITY // CS & CYBERSECURITY
hero.narrativeLead: Mohammed Kanod is a builder, experimenter, and computer science student exploring the friction between autonomous software, operating system kernels, and physical computation.
hero.narrativeSub: Curious by default. Not interested in conventional SaaS templates or safe formulas. I build prototypes to find where systems break and understand why they work.

projects.title: Memora
projects.subtitle: Personal AI Memory System
projects.oneLiner: An offline-first AI system that understands conversations by transcribing speech, identifying speakers, and reconstructing who said what.
projects.description: Memora is an experimental personal memory system built around the idea that machines should be able to remember conversations with context. The system processes audio through voice activity detection, speaker diarization, speaker recognition, and speech-to-text, transforming raw conversations into structured, speaker-aware transcripts. It combines ECAPA-TDNN speaker embeddings, cosine-similarity recognition, agglomerative clustering, and calibrated recognition thresholds to distinguish known and unknown speakers. The project explores the foundations required for a future privacy-first personal memory engine where conversations can become searchable, contextual memories rather than isolated transcripts.
highlights: Built a modular audio intelligence pipeline combining VAD, speaker diarization, speaker recognition, and speech-to-text.
Implemented speaker identification using ECAPA-TDNN embeddings with cosine similarity and configurable recognition thresholds.
Added threshold calibration using FAR, FRR, and EER to evaluate and tune speaker recognition performance.
Designed the system to support local, privacy-oriented processing without requiring cloud APIs for its core pipeline.
Built an interactive web interface for recording, uploading, processing, enrolling speakers, calibrating recognition, and exporting transcripts.
projects.takeaway: This experiment showed me that building a useful memory system starts much earlier than an LLM: the system first needs to reliably understand the real world, determine who is speaking, preserve temporal context, and retain trustworthy evidence. Memora is my exploration of that foundation.

experiments.title: VeriScope AI
experiments.oneLiner: An explainable AI system for analysing news credibility, claims, bias, and supporting evidence.
experiments.hypothesis: Can an AI system help users evaluate the credibility of news by decomposing articles into claims and analysing evidence, language, bias, and context rather than reducing them to a simple true-or-false verdict?
experiments.findings: A functional prototype and application architecture were developed around explainable news analysis, structured AI outputs, and credibility scoring. Development was paused after deployment constraints prevented reliable access to the intended AI inference API. The project remains open for future continuation with a different inference provider or deployment architecture.

principles.tagline: Why does it have to work this way?
principles.description: Standard architectures exist for historical convenience, not theoretical optimality. Always interrogate first principles before accepting standard libraries or conventional patterns.

principles.tagline: A working prototype teaches more than endless planning.
principles.description: Speculation produces debate; working software produces truth. When an architectural hypothesis is uncertain, write the minimal proof of concept and run it.

principles.tagline: The most interesting projects begin with a strange question.
principles.description: Linear goal-setting produces incremental iterations. Unconventional breakthroughs emerge when following deep technical curiosity into unfamiliar domains.

principles.tagline: If something breaks, find out why.
principles.description: A system crash or dropped packet is not an inconvenience—it is telemetry. The boundary where software behaves unpredictably reveals its true architecture.

cybersecurity.label: CYBERSECURITY
cybersecurity.narrative: When software runs as intended, it follows instructions. But when it fails under adversarial conditions, its true assumptions are revealed. I focus on kernel boundaries, memory safety, and raw protocol integrity.

about.label: BEYOND THE SCREEN
about.narrativeLead: This portfolio is not a monument to a finished expert. It is an honest, real-time chronicle of someone in the thick of learning, experimenting, and finding where the boundaries break.
about.narrativeBody1: As a Computer Science and Cybersecurity student, my formal education is the baseline, but the real insights come from late-night experiments—reading systems papers, compiling code from scratch, and reverse-engineering protocols.
about.narrativeBody2: I don't believe in fake polish. True technical understanding comes from having the patience to break things down to first principles and the stamina to rebuild them until they hold.

items.title: CYBERSECURITY & KERNEL SYSTEMS
items.detail: Deep-diving into low-level operating system boundaries, eBPF telemetry, memory safety in Rust, and network protocol defense.
